correctness.rationale: For the connected 18-vertex Pappus incidence graph, a function with positive support S and doubled set T is valid exactly when S dominates and each zero can either borrow from a neighbor in T or replace a singly occupied neighbor in S and still dominate. The independent replay exhausted 985,663 assignments of weight at most eight. Nothing below eight worked, and the 2,691 minima split as 1,755/882/54 by number of doubled vertices. Enumeration of point permutations preserving line triples and of point-to-line bijections preserving incidence gave all 216 automorphisms: connected bipartiteness makes these the only two possibilities. The orbit distributions by class are 27×1, 108×8, 216×4; 18×1, 108×2, 216×3; and 54×1, giving 20 orbits. Every unit transfer to a distinct vertex with occupancy at most one was tested against the minimum set, with graph adjacency imposed for slides. All-source BFS reproduced connectedness, 18,846 jump and 6,372 slide edges, radii and diameters (8,9) and (9,12), and the respective eccentricity counts (1,323,1,368) and (567,1,422,486,216).
residual_risks: This is an exhaustive finite calculation, not a certificate for other graphs or for successive attack-response play.

value.rationale: The Pappus graph is a standard cubic symmetric test object. The weighted optimum and transfer invariant answers a concrete question left by the secure-set census: do the doubled optima occur, and how do they change the move geometry? They constitute over a third of the optima and introduce distinct symmetry types; the exact slide diameter increases from 10 to 12 even though additional optimizers and moves are allowed. This gives a substantive finite benchmark for distinguishing jump and slide reconfiguration, not a new name for the singleton enumeration.
residual_risks: Significance is local to this graph and these reconfiguration rules; no family theorem follows.
